new_statements.quote: Described in terms of the elements distributed in it and the features which characterize it, the phonological word is the unit of stress placement in the phonological hierarchy. Each phonological word has one and only one stress. The factors that condition stress have not been studied and, as mentioned, are not the concern of this discussion. It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis in Dinka. [...] The phonological word is the level of distribution of the syllable: one syllable is stressed in each word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka is a tone language (with contrastive three-level vowel length and voice quality) whose words are overwhelmingly monosyllabic. Malou says every phonological word carries exactly one non-contrastive stress but that what determines which syllable carries it 'has not been studied'; no placement rule is given. Later work is either silent (Blum 2023, van Urk 2015, Mayom 2014 on Bor) or sceptical: van Urk & Chong (2025 ms) say Dinka 'lacks an obvious stress system' (root-final syllable is the prominent/morphology-bearing position), and Remijsen & Manyang 2009 report that Remijsen & Gilley 2008 found no acoustic support for Gilley's (2003) stress in the Rek dialect Luanyjang.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Malou explicitly leaves the conditioning of stress unstudied. Malou's example (5) marks stress on words in short phrases without stating a rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (defined as the domain bounded by potential pause); statement is for Dinka as a whole (pan-dialectal), not specifically Bor; Malou's phonological sketch also describes sentence-level intonation (declarative downdrift etc.) separately (sec. 2.1).
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand stress statement found (Malou 1988) is a pan-Dinka description covering all four major varieties (Eastern = Bor based, Northern/Padang, Southern/Agar, Western/Rek; Malou p. 1); the author is a native speaker whose own variety is not stated in the pages read (the earlier scan note calls him a Bor-area speaker; his acoustic-study speakers are labelled 'southern' and 'eastern', eastern = Bor-based in his classification). Every Bor-specific source opened (Blum 2023 on Bor South, van Urk 2015 on Bor, Mayom 2014 on Bor, Remijsen 2013 on Bor South/North) is silent on word stress. The sceptical statements (Remijsen & Manyang 2009 fn. 5; van Urk & Chong 2025 ms 'Dinka lacks an obvious stress system') concern Luanyjang/Rek (sout2832) and Agar (dib, sout... South Central) respectively, extended by the authors to Dinka generally. Sister-glottocode audit sout2832 (Southwestern Dinka) already holds the Malou file and reaches the same statement.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2 'The Phonological Word' (printed pp. 9-10, PDF pp. 26-27): the phonological word is the unit of stress placement; each phonological word has one and only one stress; the factors conditioning stress 'have not been studied'; stress is neither contrastive nor used for semantic emphasis. Pan-Dinka description by a native speaker (four varieties, Eastern = Bor based, p. 1); no placement rule.

sources.citation: Blum, Mirella, Maria Eduarda Goncalves Freitas, Chol Stephen Jok & Bert Remijsen. 2025. Dataset investigating syllable stress in Dinka. Harvard Dataverse, doi:10.7910/DVN/KBMYUZ (readme + Dataverse metadata)
sources.note: Description: 'collected in an investigation for the presence of syllable stress in the Dinka language. Ostensibly homophonous forms of short-stem and long-stem transitive verbs were collected to analyze whether any vocal effort measurements differ significantly'; recorded in Juba 2024 from Chol Stephen Jok (dialect not stated). No result reported; the paper it supplements is not named.

sources.citation: Blum, Mirella L. 2023. Aspects of cross-variety Dinka tonal phonology. PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh, 203 pp. doi:10.7488/era/3585
sources.note: Ch. 2 covers segments, syllable structure ('Dinka is largely monosyllabic... Polysyllabic words are a minority'), three-level vowel length, voice quality and tone; ch. 6 treats Bor South High~Rise alternations. 'Stress' occurs only in the reference list; Gilley 2003 is listed in sec. 1.2 among publications that are 'misleading' for not taking tone into account. No word-stress statement.
